headline: She wore yellow to Miley Cyrus’s wedding. I applaud her.
author: Michelle Singletary

paragraphs.text: My shero is the woman in yellow who inadvertently drew attention to a special occasion trend I loathe.
The fashion faux pas police pounced after a guest at Miley Cyrus and Maxx Morando’s wedding ceremony in Palm Springs, California, broke the all-black dress code by wearing a mustard-colored outfit.

Miley Cyrus wedding guest is called out for failing to adhere to strict black dress code at her star-studded nuptials as she stands out in bright yellow dress with fans asking 'who is this diva?' https://t.co/Dx5xvjHhq3— Daily Mail (@DailyMail) November 23, 2026

In the comment section of a viral Instagram post, the guest’s sister defended her, insisting it was an honest mistake. Even so, she also offered a mild critique for missing the dress directive, writing that her sibling “should have known better to double check the invite.”
“Where was the wedding planner with the black shawl to give her?” one commenter wrote.
Another wrote: “How embarrassing!”
Really?
I say hallelujah. Heck yes to the yellow dress, even if it wasn’t a deliberate act of defiance against all-too-common bossy dress code edicts.

Whether it’s a milestone birthday, an anniversary dinner or a high-profile wedding, etiquette rules suggest that hosts, as a courtesy, communicate a dress code — formal, semiformal, business — so that people don’t feel over- or underdressed.
Requiring ridiculously specific color palettes — eggshell, not cream; eggplant, not plum; blush, not pink — treats guests like photographic props.
Hosts have every right to plan a celebration that feels meaningful to them, and guests understand there will naturally be some cost and effort in showing up.
Still, genuine hospitality means keeping guests’ financial realities and comfort in mind. Here’s how.
Make it easy for them to show up
There’s a simple equation that applies to important gatherings.
My expression of affection for you is that I’m coming to your event.
Your expression of your caring for me is that you make it as easy as possible for me to attend your special celebration.
This might mean your elderly auntie with chronic back pain may not appreciate having to fly to Fiji for your three-day wedding extravaganza.

I was invited to an all-white party, but it was at the end of the summer season. I wanted to attend because it was part of a financial conference and networking was an important part of the gathering.

Stores stock darker, richer palettes during colder months, making it more difficult to find lighter shades on the rack. So to fit in, I had to shop at several stores to find something suitable for the evening affair. I could have gone rogue, but who wants to subject themselves to the chatter and criticism about not following the rules?
One gentleman at the all-white party arrived wearing the plush white robe provided by the hotel. I admired his ingenuity.
Keep affordability in mind
It’s about balance. If you want a themed event, fine. But plan it so that the cost is minimal.

I get so stressed when I receive invitations with instructions on what I should wear. I have a simple wardrobe, and these themed events often require me to purchase new clothes or accessories I might never wear again.
Many will comply with your demands even when they know it will break their budget.

A 2024 survey by LendingTree found that among the 54 percent of Americans who had attended a wedding in the last five years, 31 percent took on debt to attend. Nearly a quarter amassed $2,500 or more in debt.
Even when people’s better judgment says “RSVP no,” they go anyway. According to the survey, guests who took on the debt felt pressure from the couple, family and friends to attend.

That kind of financial strain shouldn’t be the price of admission. Make coming to your event as inexpensive as possible. You should care enough about your guests to know what they can and can’t afford.
You should not pressure people to spend past their financial comfort zone to prove you are worthy of their presence.
You pay for the extravagance

The definition of hosting has become very warped. People plan big celebrations and then charge guests to attend. And they do so under the guise that if they didn’t pass their costs on to the attendees, they wouldn’t be able to hold their massive party.
There’s nothing wrong with wanting a big, splashy event. But if you’re the host and you’re inviting people to attend, you should pay for the party.
You can have the fanciest engagement, bachelor or bachelorette party you want. But don’t push the financial burden of attending the event on your guests.
Accept a “no” or nonconformity with grace
In the LendingTree survey, 12 percent of folks who declined a wedding invitation said it ruined their relationship with the couple.

Guilt-tripping can be subtle or blunt. But if someone says they can’t afford to attend, including the need to buy a new outfit to match your color aesthetic, and you respond with comments meant to make them feel bad for declining the invitation, you are not a gracious host.
Nor should you criticize a guest who arrives wearing the wrong shade.
Don’t make people’s attendance or color-coded compliance at your affair a test.
Love does not test.
